title: Remove Element
description: Brute force to optimized: a separate survivors array versus a write pointer versus swapping with the end.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array nums and an integer val, remove every occurrence of val in place, and return the new length of the array after removal. The relative order of the remaining elements may change.

blocks.caption: A write pointer keeps only the surviving elements, compacted directly into the front of the array

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given an integer array nums and an integer val, remove every occurrence of val in place, and return the new length of the array after removal. The relative order of the remaining elements may change.

blocks.title: Analogy: Clearing Out One Specific Item From a Shelf
blocks.text: Like walking along a shelf of mixed items and pulling out every instance of one specific unwanted item, sliding the remaining items together to fill the gaps, without needing a second shelf to work from.

blocks.caption: Remove every occurrence of a value in place, reporting how many elements remain

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: nums = [3, 2, 2, 3], val = 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Removing both 3s leaves 2 and 2","in any order","Both occurrences of val (3) are removed; since order among survivors is unconstrained, [2, 2] in either order is valid"],["Answer","2, with the first 2 elements being [2, 2]","The new length reflects exactly how many elements survive after removing every val"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Removing every 2 leaves 0, 1, 3, 0, 4","in any order","All three occurrences of val (2) are removed, leaving the other 5 elements in any relative order"],["Answer","5, with the first 5 elements being those values in some order","5 elements survive out of the original 8"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: nums contains no occurrence of val at all
If val never appears in nums, nothing needs to change, and the new length is simply the original length of the array.
5. How Should We Think?

Before building any separate structure, notice the problem explicitly frees up a constraint most removal problems do not: the survivors' relative order does not need to be preserved, which opens up in-place techniques that would otherwise be impossible.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since only the final new-length prefix of the array needs to be correct, and everything past that point is irrelevant, there is no fundamental need for a second array at all, just a way to compact survivors toward the front of the same array.

Observation 2: A write pointer, always trailing at or behind the read pointer, naturally achieves this compaction: every time a surviving, non-val, element is read, it is copied to the write position and the write pointer advances; every val is simply never copied anywhere, effectively deleted.

Observation 3: Since survivor order is unconstrained, an even more surgical alternative exists: instead of shifting every element after a removed one forward by one position, which the write-pointer approach does implicitly over many steps, a matching element can be swapped directly with whatever currently sits at the very end of the still-being-considered range, and that range simply shrinks by one, needing just a single swap per match instead of a cascading shift.

Observation 4: The swap-with-end approach trades a possibly very different final order for doing less total work specifically when matches are rare, since a shift-based approach's total cost scales with how many elements come after each match, while a swap's cost per match is always exactly one write, regardless of position.

Whenever an array modification allows the survivors' relative order to change freely, look past the standard "shift everything after a hole" technique toward two sharper options: a trailing write pointer for simple linear compaction, or a swap-with-the-end technique that turns each removal into a single O(1) swap instead of a shift.

This progression, separate array, then write pointer, then swap with the end, mirrors a common theme across in-place array problems: relaxing an unnecessary constraint, like preserving order, each time unlocks a cheaper technique.
6. Brute Force Solution
Build a completely separate array containing only the elements that are not equal to val, then copy that array back over the original.
Step by step algorithm

items: Scan nums, collecting every element not equal to val into a new array.
Copy the new array back into nums.
Return the new array's length.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: survivors is built by checking every element against val independently, since deciding whether to keep an element never depends on any other element's fate.
The copy-back loop only writes as many positions as survivors actually has, since indices at or beyond that length are irrelevant to the problem's required output.
The function returns the survivors count directly, since that count is the new length the problem asks for, independent of whatever values happen to remain in the untouched tail of nums.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every element not equal to val is correctly preserved, in order, so the result is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), for the scan and the copy back.
Space: O(n), for the separate survivors array.

Limitation: building an entirely separate array is unnecessary. Since the relative order of survivors does not need to be preserved, the removal can happen directly within the original array using two pointers.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Building a whole separate array only to copy it right back into the original wastes exactly the extra space the copy-back step itself proves was never truly needed, since every value ultimately lands back in nums anyway. If the decision, "keep this element or not", is made while scanning nums itself, using one pointer to read and a second, slower-or-equal pointer to mark where the next kept element belongs, survivors can be compacted directly into the front of the same array, with no second array ever allocated. The read pointer always moves forward by one; the write pointer only moves forward when a value is actually kept, naturally leaving unwanted values overwritten or stranded past the final write position, exactly matching the requirement that only the new-length prefix needs to be correct.

Use a write pointer starting at the front of the array, and scan through with a read pointer. Whenever the current element is not equal to val, copy it to the write position and advance the write pointer. Elements equal to val are simply skipped and never copied anywhere, naturally getting overwritten or left behind past the final write position.
9. Optimized Solution
Two pointers: a read pointer scanning the whole array, and a write pointer tracking where the next surviving element belongs.
Dry run for nums = [3, 2, 2, 3], val = 3

blocks.content: {"headers":["Read index","Value","Action","Write pointer after","Why"],"rows":[["0","3","equals val, skip","0","3 matches val, so it is never copied anywhere and the write pointer does not advance"],["1","2","copy to index 0","1","2 does not match val, so it survives and is written to the current write position, advancing the pointer"],["2","2","copy to index 1","2","Another surviving 2 is written to the next write position"],["3","3","equals val, skip","2","The final 3 also matches val and is skipped, leaving the write pointer at 2, the correct final length"]]}

blocks.caption: Optimized: a write pointer keeps only the surviving elements, skipping every match of val

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(1) extra, everything happens directly within the original array.
10. Further Optimization: Swap With the End When Matches Are Rare

When val is expected to occur rarely, shifting every subsequent element forward by one for each match, which is what the write pointer approach implicitly does over many iterations, does more copying than necessary. An alternative swaps a matching element directly with whatever is currently at the very end of the considered range, then shrinks that range by one, avoiding shifting all the elements in between. This trades a possibly different relative order for fewer total writes when matches are infrequent.
Dry run for nums = [0, 1, 2, 2, 3], val = 2

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Index 0 (0), not a match, move on","range still [0, 5)","0 is not val, so it already belongs in the surviving prefix and simply gets passed over"],["Index 1 (1), not a match, move on","range still [0, 5)","1 is also not val, so it stays exactly where it is"],["Index 2 (2), a match, swap with the last element (3) and shrink the range","[0, 1, 3, 2, 2], range now [0, 4)","Rather than shifting every element after index 2 forward, the single matching value is replaced in one swap by whatever currently sits at the range's last position"],["Index 2 is now 3, not a match, move on","range still [0, 4)","The newly swapped-in value at index 2 must be checked before advancing, since it was never examined before arriving here"],["Index 3 (2), a match, swap with the new last element (3) and shrink","[0, 1, 3, 3, 2], range now [0, 3)","The considered range has shrunk to exclude the previously swapped element, and this new match is resolved the same way"],["Loop ends, new length is 3","final array (first 3 elements): [0, 1, 3]","The considered range has shrunk down to exactly the count of surviving elements"]]}

blocks.caption: Further optimization: swap a matching element with the last element instead of shifting everything

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) worst case, but performs fewer total writes than the write pointer approach when matches of val are rare.
Space: O(1) extra.
Code walkthrough

items: n starts as the full array length but shrinks every time a match is found, since the range from 0 to n always represents "elements not yet confirmed as survivors or removed".

The read index i only advances when the current element is confirmed to survive, not equal to val, since a value just swapped in from the end has not yet been checked and must be examined at the same index next.
Overwriting the matching element directly with whatever is currently the last element of the shrinking range happens in a single write, instead of shifting every element in between.
The loop naturally terminates once the read index catches up to the shrinking boundary, at which point every element from 0 up to that boundary has been confirmed a survivor.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

Both optimized approaches are the standard "in place partition" pattern, and choosing between them depends on whether matches are expected to be common, favoring the simple write pointer, or rare, favoring the swap with the end technique, which minimizes total writes.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting that the problem only cares about the first "new length" elements being correct, not the elements past that point, which is what makes the swap-with-end technique valid despite reordering elements.

Advancing the read pointer even when a swap just brought in a brand new, unchecked value at the current index in the swap-based approach, which would skip checking it entirely and could leave an undetected match in the final result.

Using the write-pointer approach's read index to also drive the swap-based approach's loop increment, conflating two structurally different techniques that advance their pointers under different conditions.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Mention both variants and the trade off between them explicitly, since recognizing that order does not need to be preserved is what unlocks the swap-with-end optimization as a legitimate alternative.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Remove elements in place, order of survivors does not matter" points toward a trailing write pointer first for simplicity, then the swap-with-end alternative as a refinement when matches are expected to be rare.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this change if the order of survivors did need to be preserved? The swap-with-end technique would no longer be valid, since it can reorder elements; only the write-pointer approach, which preserves relative order among survivors, would remain applicable.
What if val could be a whole range of values instead of a single one? Both techniques generalize directly, just replacing the equality check with a range-membership check.

How would you extend this to removing duplicates instead of a specific value, like Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array? A similar write-pointer technique applies, but the "keep" condition becomes "differs from the previously kept element" instead of "differs from a fixed val", which additionally relies on the array being sorted.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Classic "in-place partition" pattern, the same core idea behind the partition step of quicksort, separating elements into "keep" and "discard" groups without extra space.
Same "write pointer trails a read pointer" technique as Move Zeroes and Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array, all compacting survivors toward the front of the same array.
Same "trade order for fewer writes" tradeoff seen whenever a problem's constraints are relaxed just enough to allow a swap-based shortcut instead of a full shift.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (write pointer): O(n) time, O(1) space.
Further optimized (swap with the end): O(n) time worst case, O(1) space, fewer writes when matches are rare.
13. Final Summary

items: Pattern: In-place partition via a write pointer, or a swap-with-the-end refinement when matches are rare

Core Idea: Since survivors' relative order does not need to be preserved, elements can be compacted directly within the original array, either by trailing write pointer or by swapping matches with the shrinking range's last element
Time: O(n) for both optimized approaches
Space: O(1) extra for both
Most Important Observation: Relaxing an order-preservation constraint unlocks cheaper in-place techniques, from a simple write pointer to an even sparser swap-with-end approach
Interview Difficulty: Easy to Medium
One-line memory trick: Order does not matter, so compact in place: write pointer for simplicity, swap-with-end for fewer writes
